summaries.example: Imagine two students named Alex. If you say, “Alex brought the blue backpack,” your listener may ask, “Which Alex?” You might answer, “The Alex sitting by the window.” Some philosophers say the name works because of this description. Others say the name is connected to a particular person through earlier uses of the name. The situation shows that words may need names, descriptions, context, or people’s intentions to connect language with the world.
summaries.summary: Reference is the way language and other representations connect with things. This entry mainly studies language, especially expressions that seem to pick out one person or object. It asks how names refer, what names mean, and whether names work through descriptions, through chains of communication, or directly. A description such as “the student by the window” seems to identify something by its features. A different view treats a name more like a label whose connection began when someone gave it to an object and was then passed on through communication. Words such as “I,” “here,” “now,” “this,” and “that” create further problems because their reference can depend on the speaker, place, time, gestures, attention, or intentions. The entry also discusses definite descriptions such as “the book,” including whether they refer at all or merely help listeners identify a speaker’s target. It ends by comparing four broad models: description-based, causal, rule-based, and intention-based accounts. It also considers whether reference might be unclear, plural, or not one unified relation.
key_ideas: Some words can connect what we say with particular things in the world.
Philosophers disagree about whether names work like labels, descriptions, rules, or links passed between speakers.
A name can be used for more than one person, so the situation may matter.
Words such as “I,” “here,” “this,” and “that” depend strongly on who is speaking and what is happening.
Philosophers also disagree about whether every referring expression really refers in one single way.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reference helps explain how people talk about real places, objects, and people instead of making sounds with no target. It matters for everyday communication: if a name, pronoun, or description is unclear, listeners may misunderstand. Studying reference also shows why ordinary language can be more complicated than it first appears. The same word can work differently in different settings, and philosophers can reasonably disagree about which features make communication successful.

important_terms.definition: The connection between a word or other representation and the thing, person, or property it is about.
A name for a particular person, place, or thing, such as “Kyoto” or “Mount Kilimanjaro.”
Extra information used to identify something, such as “the student by the window.”
A word whose reference changes with the situation, such as “I,” “here,” or “now.”
A word like “this” or “that,” often used while pointing or directing attention.

questions_to_think_about: If two people have the same name, how do you show which person you mean?
Can you use “this” clearly without pointing?
Does knowing a name require knowing facts about the person?
Are words doing the referring, or are speakers doing it with words?

summaries.example: Suppose a speaker points toward a photograph and says, “That is a picture of a great philosopher.” The speaker intends to discuss one photograph, but the picture has secretly been replaced by another. What does “that” refer to? One theory gives priority to the speaker’s intention. Another emphasizes the gesture and the object actually indicated. A third looks to discourse structure or what is already the focus of attention. summaries.summary: The entry investigates linguistic reference: the relation by which uses of words connect with objects, people, places, or properties. It focuses especially on singular expressions, including proper names, indexicals, demonstratives, and definite descriptions. Several questions organize the discussion. Do expressions refer because speakers use them with a referring intention, or because the expressions already have reference? Is a name’s meaning exhausted by its referent, or does descriptive information contribute? Is there one general mechanism of reference, or do different expressions use different mechanisms? And how much can reference depend on private mental states? Descriptivist theories hold that a name refers through associated identifying content. They can explain why two names may provide different information even when they have the same referent, but they face challenges when speakers know too little to identify the bearer and when names behave differently from descriptions in modal claims. Millian and causal approaches treat names as direct or tag-like, with reference fixed by an initial naming and transmitted through communicative chains. Multiple bearers of one spoken or written form complicate both approaches. Pure indexicals, such as “I,” “here,” and “now,” appear to follow stable context-sensitive rules; demonstratives such as “this” and “that” may depend on gesture, salience, discourse, or intention, but each proposal faces difficulties. Definite descriptions raise a further question: whether they refer at all. The entry concludes by comparing four models and considering skeptical, particularist, and pluralist positions about reference.
key_ideas: The central issue is not merely what expressions mean, but what makes a particular use connect with a particular object.
Descriptivist theories connect names with identifying descriptions; Millian theories treat names as directly linked to their bearers.
Causal theories explain name reference through an initial naming and later communication, but repeated names create complications.
Pure indexicals can be analyzed by context-sensitive rules, while demonstratives and other impure indexicals are harder to explain.
Definite descriptions may be analyzed as non-referring descriptions, genuinely referring expressions, or expressions that pragmatically guide a listener toward a target.
The entry groups theories into descriptivist, causal, character-based, and intentionalist models, while also considering more radical views.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reference is central to understanding how language can be about the world and how speakers coordinate their thoughts with listeners. The topic connects semantics—the study of meaning—with pragmatics, communication, context, and mental intention. It also reveals why apparently simple sentences can raise deep questions. A theory must explain successful communication, mistakes, empty names, repeated names, shifting contexts, and cases where a description seems useful even though it does not literally fit its target.

important_terms.definition: The relation between a representational token, such as a word used on one occasion, and what that token is about.
The study of what makes an expression have its semantic value or referent; it concerns how reference is fixed.
The view that a name refers through descriptive information associated with a use, often information that identifies one object.
A view that treats a proper name as having its referent as its meaning, rather than referring through an identifying description.
A theory that explains a name’s reference through a chain beginning with an initial naming and continuing through communication.
A context-sensitive expression whose reference follows a regular rule, such as “I” referring to the speaker.
An expression such as “this” or “that,” whose reference may depend on gesture, attention, discourse, or intention.
The problem that unconstrained speaker intention could make a term refer to an implausibly wide range of objects.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone refer to a person using a name while knowing almost nothing about that person?
Is a name’s meaning just its referent, or does it include descriptive information?
When a speaker points at one object but intends another, which should determine reference?
Do definite descriptions refer, or do they merely help listeners find what the speaker is talking about?
Would it be better to treat reference as one unified relation or as several related practices?

summaries.example: At school, two students are named Jordan. You tell a friend, “Jordan left the science room.” Your friend asks, “Which Jordan?” You might answer, “The Jordan who forgot a blue notebook.” This supports a descriptivist idea: the description helps choose the person. But imagine you only heard the name “Jordan” from someone else and know no identifying facts. You can still ask, “Who is Jordan?” A causal theory says your use may succeed because the name was passed along through a chain of speakers connected to a person. If both Jordans are nearby, however, the situation and people’s intentions may still be needed to tell which one you mean.
summaries.summary: Reference is the connection between a linguistic expression used on a particular occasion and what that expression is about. The entry concentrates on singular expressions: terms that, when successful, pick out one object or individual. Proper names are the main testing ground. One family of views, descriptivism, says that a name refers because a speaker or community associates it with identifying information. This can explain why people sometimes distinguish between two people with the same name, and why two names for one object can carry different information. However, it has trouble explaining how speakers can use a name when they know too few facts to identify its bearer. Another family, associated with Millianism, treats a name as a direct label whose meaning is its referent. Causal theories add an account of how such labels are fixed and transmitted: an initial naming creates a link, and later speakers inherit the use through communication. Reusing a name for a new bearer shows that not every causal connection is part of the same chain. Indexicals introduce context-sensitive rules. “I,” “here,” and “now” can be linked to the speaker, location, and time, while “this,” “that,” and deictic pronouns appear to require gesture, salience, discourse, or intention. These proposals face problems when speakers and listeners attend to different things or when intentions conflict with gestures. Definite descriptions such as “the table” produce a related dispute over whether they refer, merely assert conditions such as existence and uniqueness, or pragmatically guide a listener to a target. key_ideas: Reference concerns how words become connected with things, not only what dictionary meanings they have.
Descriptivists emphasize identifying descriptions, while Millian and causal theorists emphasize direct reference and communication history.
A speaker may refer with a name even without knowing enough descriptive facts to identify its bearer.
Names with the same spoken form can have different bearers, which creates problems for simple theories.
“I,” “here,” and “now” seem to follow regular context rules, but “this,” “that,” and similar expressions are less predictable.
The entry compares four broad approaches: descriptions, causal chains, context-sensitive rules, and speaker intentions.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use reference constantly when giving directions, identifying people, asking questions, and discussing absent or imaginary things. Philosophical theories of reference help explain why communication sometimes succeeds even when speakers lack complete information, and why it sometimes breaks down when context or intentions are unclear. The debate also teaches a broader lesson: meaning may depend on public rules, social history, the world, and the minds of speakers and listeners together.

important_terms.definition: The relation that makes a word or other representation be about a particular thing, person, or property.
A word used as a name for one particular person, place, or object, such as a city or mountain.
A theory that says a name refers through information or properties associated with it that identify one bearer.
The view that a proper name functions more like a direct label than like a shortened description.
An account on which a name’s use is linked to an original naming and then passed through a communicative chain.
A context-sensitive word such as “I,” “here,” or “now,” whose reference changes with the situation.
A context-sensitive expression such as “this” or “that,” often used to direct attention to something.
The theory of what gives an expression its meaning or reference, including rules, descriptions, causes, and intentions.

questions_to_think_about: If you know only a name, can you still use it to refer?
What makes two uses of “Jordan” pick out different people?
Should the meaning of a name include facts about its bearer?
Can a pointing gesture determine what “that” refers to by itself?
Could reference be a group of related abilities rather than one single kind of relation?
